Alleviation of volatile fatty acids inhibition in anaerobic digestion of swine 
manure with nano-bubble water supplementation
Yujie Fan a, Ziyang Zhang b,c, Xiaojing Yang d, Haibo Yang a, Peng Deng a, Ziwen Zhao b,*
a College of Forestry, Henan Agricultural University, Zhengzhou, Henan, 450002, China
b South China Institute of Environmental Sciences, Ministry of Ecology and Environment, Guangzhou 510345, China
c Key Laboratory of Agro-Forestry Environmental Processes and Ecological Regulation of Hainan Province, College of Ecology and Environment, Hainan University, 
Haikou 570228, China
d School of Environmental Science and Engineering, Sun Yat-sen University, Guangzhou, China
H I G H L I G H T S
G R A P H I C A L  A B S T R A C T
• Volatile fatty acids (VFAs) inhibition 
was alleviated by nano-bubble water 
(NBW).
• NBW supplementation promoted buff­
ering capacity under VFAs inhibition.
• CH4 production was enhanced by NBW 
supplementation under VFAs inhibition.
• Activity of hydrolases and coenzyme 
F420 
were 
increased 
with 
NBW 
addition.
• Enriched microbial community and 
reinforced metabolic pathway were 
observed.
A R T I C L E  I N F O
Keywords:
Anaerobic digestion
Nano-bubble water
VFAs inhibition
Enzyme activity
Microbial community
A B S T R A C T
Nano-bubble water (NBW) was applied to anaerobic digestion (AD) to alleviate volatile fatty acids (VFAs) in­
hibition, improve the buffering capacity and CH4 production in this work. Results indicated that NBW acceler­
ated the consumption of VFAs and prevented inhibition due to VFAs accumulation. Additionally, NBW facilitated 
a rapid increase in partial alkalinity (PA) and total alkalinity (TA) as well as a corresponding rapid decrease in 
intermediate alkalinity (IA)/PA and VFA/TA, thereby improving buffering capacity and alleviating VFAs inhi­
bition. Moreover, CH4 production improved by more than 12.2% by NBW. Similarly, the activities of the 
extracellular hydrolases and coenzyme F420 increased. Besides, NBW increased the abundance of microbial 
community and strengthened the metabolic pathways of hydrogenotrophic methanogens, which could be the 
intrinsic mechanism by which NBW alleviated VFAs inhibition, improved system stability, and increased CH4 
production. This study demonstrates that NBW supplementation can be an effective method for mitigating 
frequent VFAs inhibition.
1. Introduction
Large amounts of agricultural waste such as livestock, poultry 
manure, and crop straw are generated annually worldwide. China alone 
produces more than 4.3 billion tons of agricultural waste each year 
(Aravani et al., 2022). If agricultural wastes are not effectively treated,

they not only pollute the environment but also deplete biomass re­
sources. Agricultural waste poses both environmental pollution chal­
lenges and opportunities to convert waste into biomass energy. 
Anaerobic digestion (AD), a time-tested waste treatment method, is an 
effective means of addressing the dual challenges of environmental 
pollution and resource scarcity (He et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023). 
Globally, carbon emissions and related global warming have become a 
threat to the world, mainly due to the widespread use of fossil fuels and 
the uncontrolled generation of solid waste. AD is a sustainable tech­
nology that has been recognized as a low carbon technology that com­
plements waste management and renewable energy. AD provides many 
advantages, including clean energy production, odour control, and 
pathogen inactivation (Zhang et al., 2022; Cui et al., 2022), making it a 
dual-purpose solution for environmental protection and resource recy­
cling when applied to agricultural waste treatment.
Volatile fatty acids (VFAs) is a type of fatty acid, generally composed 
of organic acids with carbon chains ranging from 1 to 6 atoms, including 
acetic acid, propionic acid, etc. High concentrations of VFAs can be toxic 
to microorganisms during the AD process, inhibiting acetate consump­
tion during the methanogenesis phase and resulting in reduced CH4 
production efficiency (Zhao et al., 2018). The optimal pH range for 
methanogenesis is typically between 6 and 8. When the pH drops below 
6, the activity of methanogens decreases due to the highly acidic envi­
ronment. During VFAs inhibition, the lowered pH further suppresses 
methanogenic activity. The inhibition of VFAs reduces the efficiency of 
agricultural waste treatment, impedes clean energy production, and 
severely limits its application in the field of agricultural waste resource 
utilization (Zhao et al., 2022). For example, in the AD process of kitchen 
waste, VFAs can easily accumulate, and high concentrations of VFAs 
inhibit the AD process (Yan et al., 2023a). Therefore, VFAs inhibition 
impedes the efficient treatment of agricultural waste, necessitating the 
adoption of scientifically proven methods to eliminate inhibition and 
improve the efficiency of agricultural waste treatment. There are many 
methods available to alleviate VFAs inhibition during AD process, such 
as the addition of alkaline agents (Zhou et al., 2023), trace elements 
(Lim et al., 2022), biochar (Zhu et al., 2022), and the combined use of 
microbial enhancers and activated carbon (Zhao et al., 2022). However, 
these traditional methods have certain limitations, such as secondary 
pollution from chemical agents, high energy consumption, high costs, 
and complexity of operation, which have not been widely applied in the 
field of agricultural waste resource utilization (Lim et al., 2022). 
Therefore, there is an urgent need to discover new methods that can 
effectively eliminate VFAs inhibition in AD process, without causing 
secondary pollution, simple operation, and cost-effective.
Whether it is wet, semi-dry, or dry AD process, water is required for 
the processes of mass transfer, energy conversion, and microbial elec­
tron transfer. If the properties of fermentation liquid can be altered to 
improve mass transfer efficiency and microbial activity, VFAs inhibition 
may be alleviated. Previous studies on water in the AD process had 
primarily focused on water content, specifically investigating the in­
fluence of total solids (TS) (Kizito et al., 2022; Abid et al., 2021). 
Although TS had an effect on the AD process, dilution with water did not 
fundamentally address the issue of VFAs inhibition and wasted water 
resources. Many previous studies in this field had focused on the effect of 
water content on the AD process. However, few studies had examined 
the impact of different water types and characteristics on the AD pro­
cess. It remains unclear whether VFAs inhibition can be mitigated by 
altering the types and characteristics of water. Nano-bubble water 
(NBW) refers to water containing a high concentration of nanometer- 
sized bubbles, ranging from a few nanometers to several hundred 
nanometers in diameter (Hou et al., 2022). This technology debuted in 
the late 1990 s and gained momentum in Japan in the early 21st century. 
The main characteristics of NBW include the reduced friction, the 
negative or positive zeta potentials, increased gas solubility in liquids, 
and the generation of free radicals (Liu et al., 2013). Liu et al., (2019)
found that NBW had superior adsorption compared to deionized water 
(DW). Additionally, the collapse of nanobubbles would produce a sig­
nificant amount of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which can enhance 
the degradability of various recalcitrant organics (Khan et al., 2014). 
Furthermore, the supplementation of NBW could improve mass transfer 
efficiency (Temesgen et al., 2017). Moreover, NBW production is simple 
to operate with low energy comsuption, and emits no chemical pollut­
ants. Despite its widespread application in various fields, such as agri­
culture (Sun et al., 2022), environmental protection (Jia et al., 2023), 
and medicine (Aoki et al., 2022), the potential of NBW has not been fully 
explored. Recently, NBW has been found to be able to promote CH4 
production during the AD process (Yang et al., 2019; Fan et al., 2020).
Considering the unique characteristics of NBW and the fact that it 
can play a positive role in the AD process, it would be of great promise in 
alleviating VFAs inhibition. Therefore, the goal was to study the alle­
viating effects of NBW on different degrees of VFAs inhibition and to 
uncover the underlying mechanisms. This study aimed to reduce VFAs 
inhibition and accelerate the AD process by developing a new pollution- 
free, low-energy and simple method. This study is the first attempt to use 
NBW to alleviate VFAs inhibition in AD. The results of this study suggest 
a new approach for alleviating VFAs inhibition and provide an innova­
tive solution to the common inhibition phenomenon.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. NBW
An NBW generator (Yuchuang Environmental Technology Co., Ltd., 
Shandong, China) was used to produce NBW. Air-NBW was used in this 
experiment because it was less expensive and more practical than O2- 
NBW, N2-NBW, H2-NBW, etc. Air (natural air, oxygen content is about 
21 %) was introduced into the NBW generator, and the specific prepa­
ration process followed the methods described in the relevant studies 
(Tang et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022). Following completion of the 
preparation process, the obtained NBW was used for subsequent 
experiments.
2.2. AD experiments
2.2.1. Raw materials
In this study, original swine manure samples were collected from a 
pig-farming facility in Guigang City, Guangdxi Province, China, and 
used as substrates. These samples were thoroughly sorted to remove 
impurities (such as feed residues, plastics) before being evenly mixed 
and stored. Digested sludge was collected from Guangzhou City, 
Guangdong Province, China. To acclimate the inoculum, the digested

sludge was cultivated using 1 L bottles with the raw swine manure 
samples (collected from the same pig-farming facility in Guigang City, 
Guangdxi Province, China) about one month until no biogas production. 
The swine manure collected was added into the 1 L bottles to achieve a 
feed-to-microorganisms (F/M) ratio of 1:1 (volatile solid (VS) basis) at 
the beginning of this inoculum domestication process. The initial pH in 
reactor was adjusted to 7.00 ± 0.05 using 2.0 M NaOH or HCl. The 1 L 
bottles used in this domestication process were placed into a tempera­
ture- controlled incubator (35 ± 2 ◦C). After the acclimation process, the 
inoculum obtained was used in subsequent experiments. The charac­
teristics of the inoculum and swine manure are presented in Table 1.
2.2.2. AD experiments
In this study, a series of identical 250 mL Schott Duran serum bottles 
were used as the reactor in this AD experiments, each with a working 
volume of 200 mL. At the beginning of the AD experiment, all 250 mL 
reactors were loaded with substrate (collected from the same pig- 
farming facility) and inoculum. The total loading of substrate and 
inoculum was 100 g. The seeding ratio (feed-to-microorganisms (F/M) 
ratio) in each reactor was maintained at approximately 1:1 (VS basis) 
and the swine manure collected from the same pig-farming facility was 
used as the substrate in this work. Initially, varying volumes of the VFAs 
standard solution (1000 mg/L) were added to 250 mL bottles to simulate 
VFAs inhibition. This study divided its participants into eight groups: R 
(0.5)Control/R(0.5)NBW; 
R(0.25)Control/R(0.25)NBW; 
R(0.125)Control/R 
(0.125)NBW; R(0)Control/R(0)NBW, where 0.5 mL, 0.25 mL, 0.125 mL, and 
0 mL of VFAs were added, respectively. To avoid introducing other 
chemical agents that could alter the microbial structure and to minimise 
interference from other factors, the pH was not adjusted throughout the 
experiment. 100 mL DW or NBW was added separately to the RControl 
and RNBW, respectively. Additionally, to ensure the initial anaerobic 
environment, nitrogen gas was flushed into all groups for 3 min before 
being placed in incubator (35 ± 2 ◦C). The reaction was stopped after 6 
days of no gas production.

2.3. Analysis methods
In this experiment, biogas production was measured every two days 
using a 60 mL airtight syringe. CH4 and other gas components were 
measured by gas chromatography (GC-8A/TCD, SHIMADZU Co., 
Japan). The VFAs content was determined by gas chromatography (GC- 
8A, SHIMADZU Co., Japan). The standard methods (APHA 2012) were 
used in this study to measure TS, VS, and total ammonia nitrogen (TAN). 
Soluble carbohydrates and proteins were determined according to the 
previous research (Fan et al., 2020). Coenzyme F420 was determined 
using previous studies (Hou et al.,2022; Delafontaine et al., 1979). 
Previous literature reports were used to determine intermediate alka­
linity (IA), total alkalinity (TA), and partial alkalinity (PA) (Sun et al., 
2016; Banks et al., 2012). Specifically, the basicity of the sample was 
determined by acid-base titration, in which PA and TA were measured at 
pH 5.75 and 4.3, respectively. IA was measured by pH titration from 
5.75 to 4.3.
On day 4, protease, alkaline phosphatase (ALP), α-glucosidase, and 
acid phosphatase (ACP) were measured based on previous studies (Yuan 
et al., 2017). Genomic DNA was extracted from the sludge samples at the 
end of digestion using the E.Z.N.A. Soil DNA Kit (OMEGA). The con­
centration and purity of extracted DNA samples were determined using a 
NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometre (NanoDrop Technologies). 16S 
rRNA were amplified using different sets of primers for the analysis of 
bacterial 
communities 
(338F(’5-ACTCCTACGGGAGGCAGCAG-3′)/ 
806R (5′-GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3′)) and archaeal communities 
(524F10extF (5′-TGYCAGCCGCCGCGGTAA-3′)/Arch958RmodR (5′YCC 
GGCGTTGAVTCCAATT-3′)) by using BMK Cloud Platform (Tang et al., 
2024).
2.4. Statistical analysis
All experiments were conducted in triplicates and data are shown as 
the mean or mean ± standard deviation. An analysis of variance 
(ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post-hoc test was conducted to identify 
the significance of the results.
3. Results
3.1. Changes in VFAs concentration
The conversion of macromolecules into soluble substrates is the rate 
limiting step. VFAs are important intermediate products of the AD 
process. In this study, the concentrations of VFAs was measured as 
shown in Fig. 1. The VFAs concentration in R(0) increased on the 4th 
day. The increase in the VFAs concentration on the 4th day was likely 
due to the consumption of soluble substrates during the hydrolysis stage, 
leading to the production of VFAs by microorganisms. Additionally, on 
the 4th day, the average concentration of VFAs in R(0)NBW was 1269 
mg/L, representing decrease of 27.7 % compared to its corresponding 
control group. This was attributed to NBW, which accelerated the con­
sumption of VFAs, resulting in lower VFAs concentrations. By the 10th 
day, the average VFAs concentration in R(0.125)NBW was 1033 mg/L, 
representing decrease of 20.8 % compared to R(0.125)Control, indicating 
that NBW enhanced the consumption of VFAs after the hydrolysis stage.
The VFAs concentration in R(0.25) increased slowly, followed by a 
rapid decrease after 16th day. This suggests that the consumption of 
VFAs in R(0.25) was severely inhibited in the initial stage of AD. The 
rapid decrease thereafter suggests a gradual relief of VFAs inhibition in 
the later stages of AD. Throughout the AD process, R(0.25)NBW was 
significantly lower than R(0.25)Control on the 10th, 16th, and 22nd days, 
indicating that NBW accelerated VFAs consumption in the hydrolysis 
acidification stage. For R(0.5)Control/R(0.5)NBW, the VFAs concentration 
did not decrease during the AD process, indicating that NBW was unable 
to effectively alleviate severe VFAs inhibition.
3.2. Changes in stability parameters
The pH is an important index for measuring the stability. The pH 
values of the eight groups were measured periodically (Fig. 2a). For R 
(0.5)Control/R(0.5)NBW, the pH throughout the AD process was below 5.3, 
indicating severe VFAs inhibition. R(0.25)Control/R(0.25)NBW experi­
enced a slow increase followed by a rapid increase and then stabilised,

indicating that these two groups experienced severe VFAs inhibition, 
which subsequently eased. Additionally, the pH of R(0.25)NBW was 
higher than R(0.25)Control on the 4th, 10th, and 16th days, indicating 
that NBW may improve the stability, thus relieving VFAs inhibition. For 
the R(0.125), the pH gradually increased to approximately 7.5, indi­
cating a minimal impact of VFAs inhibition. R(0) showed an initial 
decrease, followed by an increase and stabilisation in pH value. The 
initial decrease was due to the production of acidic substances during 
the acidification process.
Fig. 2b shows the TA content under different degrees of VFAs inhi­
bition. The initial TA content of R(0) was the highest at approximately 
1101 mg CaCO3/L, followed by R(0.125) (approximately 895 mg 
CaCO3/L), and R(0.25) and R(0.5) being the lowest at approximately 
751 mg CaCO3/L and 463 mg CaCO3/L, respectively. R(0)Control and R 
(0.125)Control were less than their respective NBW groups on the 4th, 
10th, and 16th days, implying that NBW was beneficial for increasing TA 
content when VFAs inhibition was absent or mild. Additionally, the TA 
content in R(0.5) was significantly lower than other six groups 
throughout the AD (p < 0.05), combined with a pH value below 5.3, 
indicating that severe VFAs inhibition occurred during the AD.
Fig. 2c depicts how PA content changes during the AD process. 
Similar to the trend in TA content, R(0), R(0.125), and R(0.25) groups 
showed an increasing trend in PA content during AD. On days 4 and 10, 
R(0)Control and R(0.125)Control were lower than R(0)NBW and R 
(0.125)NBW, respectively. The difference on the 4th day was significant, 
implying that NBW promoted a rapid increase in PA content. Further­
more, the PA content of R(0.25)NBW was higher than R(0.25)Control, 
indicating that NBW facilitated a rapid increase in PA content, thereby 
enhancing the buffering capacity and alleviating VFAs inhibition.
The results for the IA/PA are shown in Fig. 2d. Initially, the IA/PA 
value of R(0.25) was high, indicating poor stability owing to severe 
VFAs inhibition during the early AD process. In contrast, R(0) and R 
(0.125) were relatively small throughout the AD process, indicating a 
strong buffering capacity. It is worth mentioning that R(0.25)NBW was 
significantly higher than the respective control group on day 10, indi­
cating that NBW could facilitate rapid decreases in IA/PA. The IA/PA 
values of R(0), R(0.125), and R(0.25) initially decreased, followed by 
stabilisation, indicating a strong buffering capacity in the later stages of 
AD.
Fig. 2e shows the influence of NBW on VFA/TA under different de­
grees of VFAs inhibition. To maintain a healthy CH4 production in an 
anaerobic digester, the ratio of VFA/TA should be in the range of 0.1 to 
0.35 (Yuan et al., 2009). For R(0.5)Control/R(0.5)NBW, the VFA/TA values 
were all greater than 6.9 throughout the AD process, indicating severe 
VFAs inhibition and an extremely weak buffering capacity. Although R 
(0.25)Control/R(0.25)NBW exceeded 4.0 in the beginning, as the AD pro­
cess progressed, its VFA/TA value gradually decreased and eventually 
became less than 0.1, indicating that although it experienced severe 
VFAs inhibition in the beginning, the inhibition gradually decreased in 
the later stages of AD. The trends of R(0) and R(0.125) were similar to 
that of R(0.25), showing gradual downward trends. The values of R 
(0.125) and R(0) were low, indicating mild or no significant VFAs in­
hibition. Additionally, R(0)Control was higher than R(0)NBW on day 4, and 
R(0.125)Control and R(0.25)Control were higher than their respective 
control groups on the 10th and 16th days, indicating that NBW facili­
tated rapid decreases in VFA/TA, shortened the lag phase, and enhanced 
the buffering capacity. The trends in VFA/TA were similar to those of 
IA/PA.
In summary, when severe VFAs inhibition occurred during the AD 
process, such as in R(0.5)Control/R(0.5)NBW, NBW did not significantly 
improve the AD process stability. When VFAs inhibition was not severe, 
NBW can improve system stability and buffer capacity. Further studies 
are needed to determine the threshold for VFAs inhibition under NBW 
conditions.
3.3. Performance of biogas and CH4 production
As shown in Fig. 3, the average cumulative biogas production values 
of R(0.25)NBW, R(0.125)NBW, and R(0)NBW were 433, 413, and 348 mL/ 
g-VS, respectively, representing increases of 10.0 %, 10.7 %, and 12.9 %, 
respectively, compared to their corresponding control groups. More­
over, the difference of biogas production between RNBW and RControl was 
significant (p < 0.05). The AD processes were severely inhibited in R 
(0.5)Control/R(0.5)NBW, and NBW was unable to effectively alleviate 
VFAs inhibition.
For cumulative CH4 production, R(0.25)NBW obtained the highest 
relative cumulative CH4 production, averaging 293 mL/g-VS, repre­
senting increases of 13.1 % compared to R(0.25)Control. The cumulative 
CH4 production of R(0.125)NBW and R(0)NBW was 281 and 238 mL/g-VS, 
respectively, representing increases of 12.2 % and 12.3 %, respectively, 
compared to their corresponding control groups. In this study, CH4 
production and increment obtained from R(0)NBW (compared to R 
(0)control) were consistent with results obtained from previous studies 
using Air-NBW in AD of swine manure (Fan et al., 2020). Gonz´alez- 
García et al., (2021) found that simultaneous ammonia recovery using 
gas-permeable membranes improves the AD of swine manure and in­
creases CH4 yield to an average of 10–17 %. Yang et al., (2021) found 
that under the optimal biochar dosage of 5–10 %, CH4 yield was

significantly improved by 25 % in AD of swine manure. Therefore, the 
supplementation of NBW can also effectively increase CH4 production 
during AD of swine manure compared to other methods. Moreover, this 
method does not require too much energy or complex devices, and does 
not consume chemicals or produce pollution. Due to severe VFAs inhi­
bition, CH4 production was severely affected in R(0.5). Moreover, the 
difference of CH4 production between RNBW and RControl was significant 
(p < 0.05). Economic assessment was used in this study, where the 
heating value of CH4 is 40.03 kJ/L under 1 atm and 25 ◦C (Silva et al., 
2018). The results showed that the supplementation of NBW resulted in 
604.30kWh of electricity generated by processing one ton of swine 
manure in this study, which was significantly better than the control 
group (Table 2).
It is worth mentioning that R(0.125) were higher than those of R(0), 
which was likely due to the supplementation of VFAs in R(0.125) 
providing organic acids for the AD process and increasing the nutrient 
content available for microorganisms. Interestingly, although R 
(0.25)NBW exhibited the highest cumulative biogas and CH4 production, 
its increase was less than of R(0.125)NBW, which was insufficient to 
compensate for the doubling of the VFAs addition, indicating that severe 
VFAs inhibition was detrimental to biogas and CH4 production.
3.4. Performance of TAN, FAN, and soluble organics
In this study, TAN content was measured to clarify whether ammonia 
inhibition occurs during the AD process and whether it synergistically 
interacts with VFAs inhibition. As shown in Fig. 4a, the TAN content in 
RNBW and RControl were less than 1200 mg/L. Therefore, none of the 
groups in this study experience ammonia inhibition. The FAN content in 
RNBW and RControl were less than 40 mg/L (Fig. 4b), indicating that none 
of the groups experienced FAN inhibition according to previous reports 
on the threshold for FAN (De Baere et al., 1984). Furthermore, because 
the pH values of R(0.5)Control/R(0.5)NBW were less than 5.3, the FAN 
contents of these two groups were minimal. Overall, no inhibition of 
ammonia was observed in this study.
Fig. 4c shows the performance of the soluble proteins. Except for R 
(0.5), the soluble proteins of the other six groups initially increased, then 
decreased, and eventually stabilised. This increase was most likely 
caused by hydrolysis, which increased soluble protein production. 
Compared to R(0) and R(0.125), the decrease in soluble proteins in R 
(0.25) was slower, possibly because VFAs inhibition partially hindered 
the consumption of soluble proteins. The soluble proteins of RControl 
were lower than their respective RNBW on the 4th day, indicating that 
NBW accelerated the production of soluble proteins. The trends in sol­
uble carbohydrates were similar to those in soluble proteins (Fig. 4d). 
Due to severe VFAs inhibition, R(0.5) was not significantly consumed. 
The soluble carbohydrates of R(0.125) and R(0.25) increased initial, 
then decreased, and eventually stabilised. R(0) gradually declines and 
then stabilises.

3.5. Enzyme activity performance
Enzymes are essential components of the AD process, serving 
important functions throughout the process. This study investigated the 
activities of enzymes in two limiting steps of AD: hydrolysis and meth­
anogenesis. A comparative study was conducted on extracellular hy­
drolytic enzymes such as ACP, ALP, α-glucosidase, and proteases. Fig. 5a 
shows that the four extracellular hydrolytic enzymes in RNBW were more 
active than RControl with enzyme activity increased by 3.3 % to 15.2 % in 
different groups. This phenomenon indicated that NBW enhanced the 
activity of hydrolytic enzymes, thereby accelerating the hydrolysis 
process under VFAs inhibition. Subsequently, F420, which reflects the 
activity of methanogens, was evaluated in this work. The results showed 
that F420 in RNBW were more active than RControl with enzyme activity 
increased by 8.7 % to 21.1 % in different groups (Fig. 5b). Therefore, 
NBW can enhance the activity of extracellular hydrolytic enzymes and 
coenzyme F420, thereby accelerating the hydrolysis and methanogenic 
stage.
3.6. Microbial community structure
To uncover the underlying mechanisms and gain a deeper under­
standing of the microbial community structure under different degrees 
of VFAs inhibition, we performed high-throughput sequencing analysis. 
The archaeal and bacterial diversity results are shown in Table 3 and 4. 
The coverage indices exceeded 0.99, indicating that the sequencing data 
covered almost all the sequences in the samples.
In archaeal sequencing, as indicated by the Chao and Ace indices, the 
abundances of archaeal microbial communities in RNBW were higher 
than those in control groups, indicating that NBW was conducive to 
improving the performance of archaeal microbial communities in the 
AD process. Additionally, as VFAs inhibition intensified, the abundance 
of archaeal microbial communities in RNBW gradually increased, and the 
increase was relatively larger than that in the corresponding control 
groups, implying that NBW helped alleviate VFAs inhibition on archaea. 
Furthermore, the Shannon and Simpson indices of R(0.25)NBW were the 
highest, indicating that the archaeal microbial diversity of R(0.25)NBW 
was the highest and further demonstrating the positive effects of NBW 
on archaeal biodiversity.
The dominant phyla were Abditibacteriota, Acidobacteriota, Actino­
bacteriota, and Bacteroidetes (Fig. 6a), which ferment polysaccharides in 
the AD systems and participate in the degradation of macromolecular 
organics (Strąpo´c et al., 2011). At the genus level, Sulfurovum belongs to 
autotrophic facultative sulfur-oxidizing bacteria, which can oxidize 
sulfides using oxygen or nitrate as electron acceptors to produce energy 
(Yan et al., 2023b). Sulfur-oxidizing bacteria and methanogens com­
plement each other in nutritional metabolism (Nie et al., 2021). Sul­
furovum showed an initial decreasing trend, followed by an increase 
with increasing VFAs concentrations (Fig. 6b), indicating that high VFAs 
concentrations are unfavorable for CH4 production. The genus f_bacter­
oidetes_vadinHA17 is a facultative anaerobic denitrifying bacterium 
capable of degrading various complex organic compounds in AD sys­
tems. Studies have shown that an increase in f_bacteroidetes_vadinHA17 
content can ferment more complex organic compounds, such as steroids, 
to accelerate reaction rates (Baker et al., 2020). Fig. 6a shows that 
f_bacteroidetes_vadinHA17 was higher in RNBW than RControl, which could 
explain why NBW increased hydrolysis rate and CH4 production.
Hydrogenophilaceae are denitrifying bacteria that play important 
roles in nitrogen reduction. Compared with the control group, Hydro­
genophilaceae in RNBW was enriched to a certain extent. With an increase 
in VFAs concentration, Hydrogenophilaceae in RNBW gradually decreased, 
indicating that NBW was conducive to Hydrogenophilaceae in the AD 
process when VFAs inhibition was not severe. Additionally, Anaeroli­
neaceae, a representative family of Chloroflexi, not only has denitrifi­
cation functions but also participates in the degradation of 
carbohydrates (Sun et al., 2015). Anaerolineaceae initially increased and 
then decreased with increasing VFAs concentrations in both RControl and 
RNBW, indicating that severe VFAs inhibition was unfavourable for

have aided CH4 production and denitrification. Although high concen­

Crenarchaeota accounted for the largest proportion, with relative 
abundances ranging from 30.10 % to 40.50 %. Halobacterota was the 
second most dominant phylum, accounting for approximately 16.80 % 
to 23.50 %, whereas Euryarchaeota accounted for approximately 9.50 % 
to 14.90 %. The dominant archaeal genera were Methanosaeta, c_Bath­
yarchaeia, o_unidentified_archaeon, uncultured_methanogenic_archaeon, 
Methanobacterium, and Candidatus_Methanfastidiosum (Fig. 6d). Meth­
anosaeta is a common acetate-type CH4-producing bacterium in CH4- 
producing systems, and it was enriched in all groups. Additionally, 
Methanobacterium is a hydrogenotrophic methanogen (HM), whose pri­
mary sources of energy are CO2 and H2. It was more enriched in RNBW 
than in their respective control groups, indicating that both NBW and 
control groups relied primarily on the acetate-type CH4 production 
pathway and that NBW improved the HM metabolic pathway.
To conclude, the three dominant phyla involved in CH4 production 
Halobacterota, Euryarchaeota, and Crenarchaeota. Methanosaeta was 
relatively abundant across the genus level, indicating that acetate-type 
CH4 production was the primary pathway. Furthermore, Meth­
anobacterium was more enriched in the NBW groups, suggesting that 
NBW improved the HM metabolic pathway.
4. Conclusion
This study demonstrated that the inhibition of VFAs on manure AD 
could be mitigated through the supplementation of NBW, which 
enhanced buffering capacity and CH4 production. Mechanism analysis 
indicated that NBW improved the consumption of VFAs, thereby alle­
viating the inhibitory effects caused by VFA accumulation. Additionally, 
NBW facilitated a rapid increase in pH, TA and PA during the early 
stages of the AD process, along with a swift decrease in the IA/PA and 
VFA/TA ratios. Moreover, NBW significantly increased CH4 production 
under VFAs inhibition. For microorganisms and enzymes, NBW elevated 
the activity of key enzymes (including 4 hydrolytic enzymes and coen­
zyme F420) under VFAs inhibition, enriched microbial community 
abundance, and strengthened HM metabolic pathways. These findings 
indicate the potential of NBW technology to serve as an alternative 
method for alleviating inhibition in agricultural AD systems. This study 
innovatively proposes the application of NBW to alleviate VFAs inhibi­
tion, which is common in AD of agricultural waste. This study highlights 
the potential of NBW to reduce VFAs inhibition and improve the effi­
ciency of agricultural waste treatment. Given these promising results, 
NBW technology may hold significant potential for future applications 
in AD processes under VFAs inhibition and warrants further research.
